issues.issue: The Initial Period ends eight months after delivery of the Master Recordings comprising the "Recording Obligation", a term the agreement never defines (paragraph 2.02 defines only "Minimum Recording Obligation"). The end date of the Term therefore turns on an undefined phrase.

The warranty that Artist will record "exclusively for Grantor and PRI" sits awkwardly with PRI's engagement of Grantor to furnish "exclusive services", leaving the scope of the exclusivity (and to whom it runs) open.

"To the best of their ability" and "first-class standards for production in the Phonograph Record industry" are undefined performance benchmarks with no measurable content. A court would have to supply the standard.

PRI may disapprove a Composition for defamation, libel or infringement "or which is subject to Objection for any other legal reason whatsoever", and may disapprove a studio if its use "would otherwise in any way substantially hinder or prevent" recording; these catch-alls sit against the enumerated specifics and their reach is uncertain.

Masters must be "technically satisfactory" and embody Recordings that are "first-class (as that term is understood in the record industry)"; whether a delivery qualifies is left to an undefined industry standard that both sides could read differently. This is the classic acceptance-standard ambiguity in recording agreements.

"Reasonably consistent in concept and style" and "similar in general artistic concept and style" set a purely subjective artistic benchmark with no ascertainable boundary. A dispute over whether a delivered Album complied would turn entirely on that phrase.

Delivery dates "may be reasonably extended" if the parties "mutually agree in writing, based on good business judgment" — an agreement-to-agree qualified by two undefined standards. Whether either party could refuse an extension is unresolved.

Paragraph 4.01(d)(i) says late delivery within sixty days is not a failure to comply or a breach, but paragraph 6.01(c) reduces the Advance by 10% per month from "the last date such Album would otherwise be timely delivered pursuant to paragraph 4.01". Whether the sixty-day grace shifts that Final Date cannot be resolved from the two provisions read together.

Saying the "delivery date ... shall be suspended until such time as the parties so agree" is imprecise — a date cannot be suspended, and the clause gives no outer limit or mechanism if the parties never agree on the co-producer. The effect on the Contract Period and the Term is left open.

"Satisfactory completion" of the Article 3 and 4 procedures is made the condition of delivery without saying whose satisfaction governs or by what standard. The final clause then deems accepted and released Masters to count, which cuts against the preceding non-waiver language.

The second sentence is syntactically muddled: "if the parties do not reach such agreement or if neither party gives notice ... as provided above earlier than thirty (30) days prior to the date of initial release" leaves it unclear whether the thirty-day qualifier attaches to the notice or to the deemed date. The deemed delivery date therefore cannot be computed with confidence.

Masters are declared "work made for hire" and, in the alternative, assigned; whether a recording by an independent Grantor can qualify as a work made for hire is a recurring point of construction. The belt-and-braces drafting invites a dispute over which characterisation controls.

The chapeau of 5.01(b) confines the sub-clauses to "sales of Records in the United States during the Term", yet paragraph 3.03 makes PRI's use of out-takes subject to 5.01(b)(i) generally, leaving the territorial and temporal reach of the out-take consent unclear.

"A label used by PRI ... for Recordings of PRI's top 'pop' artists then under exclusive term contract" is a vague and shifting description, and whether a heavy-metal artist's Album falls within a "pop" label commitment is contestable. The obligation cannot be applied without construing "top 'pop' artists".

"Premium use" is not defined anywhere in the provision, and paragraph 7.05(a) separately prices "premium Records" without defining them either. The scope of the consent right turns on an undefined term.

Grantor is given approval over the Artwork, yet "any matter other than the Album cover layout and the picture or art to be used on the cover" is left to PRI's sole discretion; the boundary between the approved "Artwork" and PRI's reserved matters is uncertain.

The provision first limits PRI's exemption to sales "occurring prior to PRI's receipt of such notice" and then, in the same sentence, states PRI "shall have no liability by reason of such sales at any time", which swallows the obligation entirely. The two limbs cannot both be given effect.

The chapeau of paragraph 5.01(b) confines its sub-clauses to "sales of Records in the United States during the Term", yet this sub-clause governs sales of Albums outside the United States. The two cannot be squared on their face.

Editing costs are said to be "at PRI's expense" and yet "shall constitute an Advance hereunder", i.e. recoupable from Grantor's royalties; those two characterisations point in opposite directions. Who ultimately bears the cost is genuinely open.

The clause excludes such costs from "the applicable Recording Fund provided for in paragraph 6.01", but paragraph 6.01 establishes Advances and contains no "Recording Fund". The cross-reference has no referent in the instrument.

Paragraph 5.01(d)(viii) gives PRI and its licensees "the continuing right at all times" to manufacture and sell recompilation Albums, expressly subject only to 5.01(b)(ix)(B), which appears to override the three-Album ceiling imposed by this provision. The two rights cannot readily be harmonised.

The provision gives Grantor "five (5) business days" to object but later refers to "said five (5) day period", so the length of the objection window is internally inconsistent. That mismatch changes whether an objection was timely.

The compact-disc release obligation applies only "if commercially possible", an undefined and highly elastic qualifier that could excuse performance almost entirely. Whether the obligation binds at all turns on that phrase.

All of Grantor's protections in 5.01(b) fall away if Grantor has not "Materially fulfilled" its Article 3 and 4 delivery obligations, a materiality standard nowhere defined. The trigger for losing a substantial package of rights is left to construction.

The release remedy is conditioned on Grantor having "fulfilled all of its material obligations hereunder", an undefined standard, and the cure/termination sequence uses overlapping thirty- and sixty-day periods whose starting points are hard to fix. Both sides could reasonably compute the deadlines differently.

The condition is that Grantor obtain "all consents required by PRI" and "all agreements which PRI may require", giving PRI an unbounded ability to defer the reassignment right conferred by 5.01(c). The limits of what PRI may "require" are undefined.

This tail-piece excludes November and December from the computation while the parallel tail-piece to paragraph 5.01(d) excludes October, November and December; the two adjacent suspension rules use different exclusions without explanation. A party could argue the discrepancy is a drafting slip.

The Release Territories include "Benelux" and "Scandinavia", neither of which is defined, while paragraph 7.03(c) instead names Sweden and Denmark individually; which countries trigger the release obligation is therefore uncertain. The scope of the obligation turns on those undefined regional labels.

The clause carves out liability for manufacture "occurring before PRI's receipt of such notice" and then adds that PRI "shall have no liability by reason of such manufacture at any time", which negates the whole undertaking. The two limbs of the same sentence contradict each other.

The "continuing right at all times" to manufacture and sell recompilation Albums is made subject only to paragraph 5.01(b)(ix)(B), and so appears to override the three-Album "Greatest Hits" ceiling in paragraph 5.01(b)(ix)(A). Whether the ceiling survives this provision is genuinely open.

This suspension rule excludes October, November and December while the parallel rule closing paragraph 5.01(c) excludes only November and December. The unexplained divergence between two adjacent computation rules invites argument that one is a slip.

The sentence covers "each of the first Albums ... and ... each of the second Albums ..." but then attaches a single "but only if" sales/chart condition, leaving it unclear whether the condition qualifies the second Albums alone or both. Whether PRI owes a Video for a first Album turns on that reading.

Concert Video terms are to be "negotiated in good faith" while "neither party shall be deemed obligated to reach any such agreement or to grant its consent" — an agreement to agree that gives a court nothing to enforce. The content of the good-faith duty is left undefined.

The power of attorney is triggered where Grantor "unreasonably refuses to do so and/or fails to return the same to PRI within ten (10) days"; the "and/or" leaves it unclear whether mere lateness, without unreasonableness, suffices. The scope of PRI's self-help right turns on that connector.

This paragraph grants PRI a perpetual right to use Artist's name and likeness "in connection with other merchandising of any kind", while paragraph 5.04(c) has Grantor "expressly reserve[] the right to exploit Artist's name, likenesses and biographies in all forms of merchandising". The two grants cover the same subject matter in opposite directions.

Likenesses supplied by Grantor are "deemed approved by Grantor" until notice, yet the final sentence excuses "any inadvertent failure by PRI to obtain the aforesaid approval" from being a breach, hollowing out the approval right. What remedy Grantor has for an unapproved use is unclear.

Grantor's reservation of "all forms of merchandising" cannot be squared with paragraph 5.04(a), which grants PRI a perpetual right to use the same names and likenesses "in connection with other merchandising of any kind". Which party may exploit merchandising rights is left genuinely contradictory.

The identity of Grantor's "current arrangement" counterparty is illegible/blank in the executed text, and the condition "provided PRI at the time has in the past and can arrange a 'first-class' merchandising activity" is ungrammatical and unmeasurable. Whether the Matching Right ever attaches cannot be determined from the words.

Advances are payable in instalments "promptly following" notice of commencement of recording, of mixing and of delivery, with no definition of "promptly" and no outside date. Timeliness of each instalment is left to construction.

Grantor is made responsible for "all Recording Costs", yet paragraph 3.02 requires PRI to approve the recording budget and to schedule and book studio time, and paragraph 6.01(b) fixes Advances by reference to that budget. Where responsibility for costs incurred under a PRI-controlled booking falls is not resolved.

The 10%-per-month reduction runs from "the last date such Album would otherwise be timely delivered pursuant to paragraph 4.01", but paragraph 4.01(d)(i) provides that delivery within sixty days of the stated date is not a failure to comply. Whether the Final Date includes that sixty-day grace is a genuine conflict.

The first sentence conditions Advance treatment of payments made on Grantor's behalf on PRI "obtain[ing] Grantor's prior approval", and the second says PRI "shall not be obligated to consult with Grantor" before making such payments, which are switched terms (approval versus consultation). The two sentences do not fit together.

Cross-collateralisation with the Polydor Agreements interacts with the Article 7 preamble, under which no royalties are payable "until such time as all Advances ... have been repaid"; whether Polydor advances count toward that condition is not stated. The two provisions leave the recoupment pool undefined.

Half of the $160,000 tour support is declared "non-returnable, non-recoupable" and "not Advances", but the provision says nothing about the status of the other half. The silence leaves the treatment of the balance open.

The preamble says no royalties accrue or are payable until all Advances "have been repaid to PRI", language of repayment rather than recoupment from royalties, which is circular if royalties cannot accrue until the Advances are repaid. The parenthetical "(except for accounting purposes)" does not resolve the circularity.

Paragraph 8.01 requires PRI to pay accrued royalties semi-annually "less Advances or other recoupable amounts hereunder", which assumes royalties accrue and are netted, contrary to this preamble's bar on any accrual until Advances are repaid. The two accounting mechanics differ.

The 11% rate applies to "Net Sales of all Albums sold by PRI for distribution through Normal Retail Channels in the United States"; whether a given exploitation (in particular new digital configurations) is an Album "sold" through "Normal Retail Channels" or is instead a licensed use is genuinely open on these words. The whole royalty owed turns on that characterisation.

This rate cannot be reconciled with paragraph 7.06(a), which fixes 50% of PRI's net receipts for licences of Master Recordings; a single exploitation can plausibly be described as both an Album sold through Normal Retail Channels and a licence, and the agreement gives no priority rule. Which paragraph governs is the core construction question.

"In excess of one hundred thousand (100,000) units" does not say whether the escalated 12% applies only to units above the threshold or retroactively to all units. That is a recurring escalation ambiguity.

As with 7.02(b), "in excess of two hundred fifty thousand (250,000) units" leaves open whether the 13% rate applies only to the excess units or to all units once the threshold is passed. The computation of royalties turns on that reading.

The flat 14% Japan rate sits alongside paragraph 6.04(a), which cross-collateralises this agreement with the Polydor K.K. (Japanese) recording agreements, leaving it unclear which instrument governs royalties on Japanese sales. That overlap is not addressed anywhere.

This list names Sweden and Denmark individually, while paragraph 5.01(d) uses the undefined collective "Scandinavia" for the same region; the instrument treats the territory inconsistently. Which countries belong where is left unresolved.

PRI may elect, "at its sole discretion", between a penny-rate royalty tied to an "equivalent Record not in the form of a compact disc" and a percentage of the compact disc Royalty Base; neither "equivalent Record" nor "other new Record configuration" is defined. Which configurations are captured, and what the equivalent is, is left open.

The parties are to "negotiate in good faith regarding an adjustment" of the compact disc royalty "taking into account industry-wide standards" — an agreement to agree with no fallback beyond continuing 7.04(a). What good faith requires here has no ascertainable content.

"Premium Records, Budget Records, or Records other than Albums not otherwise specifically referred to herein" is a residual catch-all set against enumerated categories, and it is unclear whether the qualifier "not otherwise specifically referred to herein" modifies all three items or only the last. Whether a given configuration falls into this half-rate bucket rather than a specific rate turns on that reading.

This residual half-rate provision overlaps with paragraph 7.02(a)'s full album rate and paragraph 7.06(a)'s 50%-of-net-receipts rate, and the agreement supplies no priority rule for a Record that answers to more than one of them. Which royalty governs a novel configuration is not resolved by the instrument as a whole.

The denominator is "the Royalty Base applicable to PRI's or its licensees' top-line single-disc LPs", an undefined and moving benchmark that neither party can fix in advance. The multiple-record royalty cannot be computed without construing it.

The 50%-of-net-receipts categories are enumerated but end with open-ended language — "licenses of Master Recordings on a flat-fee basis" and distribution "by any combination of the methods set forth above or other methods" — so the reach of the catch-all against the listed specifics is genuinely uncertain. Whether a particular exploitation (notably licensed digital distribution) falls inside this paragraph is exactly what the words leave open.

This paragraph cannot be reconciled with paragraph 7.02(a), which pays 11% of the Royalty Base for Albums sold through Normal Retail Channels; one and the same exploitation can be described as a licence under 7.06(a) and a sale under 7.02(a), and no provision states which prevails. That conflict determines the royalty rate.

"Net receipts" is defined after deduction of amounts PRI must pay third parties "such as, without limitation, production costs ... mechanical copyright payments, AFofM and other union or guild payments" — an open-ended deduction catch-all against enumerated examples. What else PRI may deduct is unbounded.

The proviso caps non-royalty-bearing club Records at "fifty percent (50%) of the Records distributed hereunder through such clubs", but does not say what royalty applies once the cap is exceeded, and "cumulative basis" is left unexplained. The remedy for breach of the cap is unstated.

This affiliated-licensee direct-marketing rate of 5% overlaps with paragraph 7.06(a)(ii), which pays 50% of net receipts for the same distribution methods when licensed to Non-Affiliated Third Parties; whether a particular licensee is "affiliated" is nowhere defined. The dividing line between the two rates is left to construction.

PRI may hold "reasonable reserves" subject to percentage caps and a liquidation schedule, but "reasonable" is not defined and PRI may adopt "such other accounting periods as PRI may in general adopt". Both the size of reserves and the accounting cycle are left to one party's judgment.

Statements become "binding" and unobjectionable after three years, yet paragraph 8.05(a) allows suit within four years of the statement, so a claim can be timely under 8.05(a) while already barred under 8.03(a). The two limitation regimes cannot be fully harmonised.

Statements are deemed "conclusively" rendered on the 8.01 due date unless Grantor objects within thirty days, which starts the three-year clock in 8.03(a) and the four-year clock in 8.05(a) from a date on which no statement may in fact have been sent. Its interaction with those two limitation provisions is not worked out.

The audit right covers "the six (6) accounting periods prior to such audit" but may be exercised "only within three (3) years after the date when PRI is required to send" the statement; six semi-annual periods is three years, so the two limits may or may not coincide depending on when the audit begins. The audit window is not clearly fixed.

The four-year contractual limitations period runs "from the date such statement of accounting for royalties or such payment was rendered", which does not say what happens where several statements or payments relate to the same royalties. The accrual date for a continuing under-accounting is left open.

The four-year suit period cannot be squared with paragraph 8.03(a), under which statements become binding and immune from objection after three years; a suit brought in year four would concern a statement Grantor is deemed to have approved. Which period controls is a genuine internal inconsistency.

The limitation is disapplied "in the event any court determines fraud or gross negligence on the part of PRI", yet the same clause purports to deny the court "authority to consider any other issues" — so the court can only find fraud by first exceeding the authority the clause allows it. That circularity leaves the carve-out's operation unclear.

The rate is the "Statutory Rate prevailing at the time of release in the applicable country", but the provision covers both the United States and Canada, which have different statutory regimes, and "Statutory Rate" is not defined in this Article. The applicable rate must be construed.

Copyright royalties are payable on 50% of "Album free goods, as defined in paragraph 13.15(a)(ii) below" but not on Albums "distributed pursuant to special sales plans", a phrase left undefined and standing against the defined free-goods category. The line between the two distributions is not drawn.

Public-domain arrangements are royalty-free unless the arranged version "varies substantially from the original work", an undefined threshold that determines whether any mechanical royalty is owed. The test invites competing readings.

The provision breaks off mid-sentence at "Mechanical royalty reserves maintained by PRI against anticipated returns", so the liquidation rule for those reserves is missing from the text. The incomplete sentence leaves the reserve mechanic unstated.

The 30%/40% mechanical reserve caps mirror the record-royalty reserve caps in paragraph 8.01 but come with no liquidation schedule of the kind 8.01 prescribes, so it is unclear whether 8.01's liquidation timetable applies to mechanical reserves. The two reserve regimes do not fit together.
